questions.question: What identifies a path domain in this lecture?
options: A) Inputs necessarily producing the same numeric output
B) Inputs executing the same program path
C) All files with one extension
D) All outputs of the system
questions.explanation: A path domain groups inputs by execution/computation sequence.

questions.question: The intended path executes, but an arithmetic result is wrong. What is this?
questions.explanation: Computation errors concern the calculation on the correct path.

questions.question: An input executes the wrong path because of a faulty condition. What is this?
questions.explanation: The input has been misclassified into the wrong path domain.

questions.question: What makes domain testing fault-oriented?
options: A) It selects inputs to expose a specified class of domain faults
B) It avoids any assumption about defects
C) It tests only interface timing
questions.explanation: The boundary-error model drives input selection.

questions.question: After c=x+y, the predicate c>5 becomes what?
questions.explanation: Substitute the assignment without changing the comparison.

questions.question: On the P1-true path, d=c-x/2 and P2 is d>=c+2. Which real-arithmetic constraint follows?
questions.explanation: Cancel c and solve -x/2>=2.

questions.question: On the P1-false path, d=c+x/2 and P2 is d>=c+2. Which constraint follows from the displayed code?
questions.explanation: Cancel c to obtain x/2>=2. The slide's x>4 wording omits equality.

questions.question: For codedomain x=4,y=0, what are the P1,P2 outcomes?
questions.explanation: c=4 gives false; d=6 and 6>=6 gives true. This follows the code rather than the slide typo.

questions.question: Which input lies in TT for the displayed codedomain predicates?
questions.explanation: Its sum exceeds 5 and x<=-4.

questions.question: Which input lies in FF for the displayed codedomain predicates?
questions.explanation: Its sum is at most 5 and x<4.

questions.question: Which operator describes a closed inequality boundary?
questions.explanation: Equality belongs to a closed boundary.

questions.question: For x+y>5, does a point with x+y=5 belong to the selected domain?
options: C) Only if x is positive
D) Only if y is positive
questions.explanation: The strict operator excludes equality.

questions.question: Under the slides' terminology, when is a domain called closed?
options: B) Any one boundary is closed
C) All its boundaries are closed
D) All boundaries use strict inequalities
questions.explanation: Keep this course definition distinct from the slide's broad use of open domain.

questions.question: What is an extreme point in the lecture?
options: A) An intersection of two or more boundaries
B) Any point far from zero
D) The point with largest test ID
questions.explanation: Boundary intersections can need special attention.

questions.question: Changing x<=10 into x<10 creates which defect?
questions.explanation: The geometric boundary stays at 10 but equality membership changes.

questions.question: Changing x+y>4 into x+y>5 creates which defect?
questions.explanation: The constant changes while the boundary normal remains the same.

questions.question: Changing x+0.5y>5 into x+y>5 creates which defect?
questions.explanation: A changed coefficient changes the line's orientation.

questions.question: Can an assignment before a predicate cause a domain error?
options: A) Only if the program has no inputs
B) Yes, if it changes the value used for classification
C) No, assignments never influence control flow
D) No, only the relational operator can matter
questions.explanation: Faulty data feeding a condition can move the effective boundary.

questions.question: Removing a required boundary constraint can cause what?
options: B) Guaranteed shrinkage in every case
C) A missing-boundary defect and possible domain enlargement
questions.explanation: Dropping a constraint may admit inputs previously excluded.

questions.question: For a closed domain boundary, where is an exact ON point?
options: A) Always inside a different domain
C) On the boundary and included
questions.explanation: Closed inequalities include their equality points.

questions.question: For a closed boundary, where should the OFF point be?
options: A) At an arbitrary extreme point
C) Exactly on the included boundary
questions.explanation: The slide's OFF choice crosses to the nearby exterior side.

questions.question: For an open boundary, where is an exact ON point?
options: A) Nowhere because open boundaries have no geometric line
C) On the boundary but excluded from the domain
questions.explanation: The boundary exists geometrically even though equality is excluded.

questions.question: For an open boundary, where should its OFF point be?
options: A) Exactly on the excluded boundary
C) Always identical to the ON point
questions.explanation: Membership is reversed relative to the closed-boundary case.

questions.question: What is the lecture's per-boundary test-selection pattern?
questions.explanation: Two distinct ON points and a nearby OFF point target boundary faults.

questions.question: Why select two distinct ON points rather than only one?
options: A) To improve sensitivity to a boundary tilt
B) To turn an open domain into a closed one
C) To avoid evaluating the predicate
D) To guarantee all nonlinear defects are detected
questions.explanation: A line can rotate around one sampled point; another point helps expose the change.

questions.question: For D:x+y>=10 with real-valued inputs, which is an appropriate nearby OFF point?
questions.explanation: Its sum is just below 10, outside the closed domain.

questions.question: For D:x+y<10 with real-valued inputs, which is an appropriate nearby OFF point?
questions.explanation: The lecture uses an interior near-boundary point for an open domain.

questions.question: For the closed domain x+7y>=6, is (0,0.858) inside or outside?
options: A) Not a valid pair of coordinates
C) Outside, since every rounded point is outside
questions.explanation: The slide's final outside wording conflicts with its arithmetic; evaluate the actual inequality.

questions.question: Which integer distinguishes intended x<=10 from faulty x<10?
questions.explanation: Only equality changes membership for this closure fault.

questions.question: Why keep the other domain constraints satisfied while testing one boundary?
options: A) To isolate that boundary's classification effect
B) To turn all inequalities into equalities
C) To avoid all boundary inputs
D) To force every path to be identical
questions.explanation: Violating another constraint may hide the boundary fault under study.
